Multi-omics of Breast Cancer

mRNA, miRNA and protein from the same tumours: quality control, differential expression and volcano plots, multi-omics integration and machine learning. Theory, full Python code, real outputs and interpretation on one page.

The question. What changes when breast tissue becomes cancer, do the molecular layers agree, and can a computer tell the breast-cancer subtypes apart from omics data?

Prepared by Dr. Avinash Gopa, Avyagraha Research and Analytics LLP (www.aviqlabs.com)

OVERVIEW

The project at a glance

Real data. The Cancer Genome Atlas breast cancer study (TCGA-BRCA), downloaded from the UCSC Xena GDC hub. 863 tumours + 112 normals with RNA-seq; 854 tumours with mRNA and miRNA and protein. Nothing is simulated.

PART A

Theory: the ideas behind the project

No code yet. These are the concepts every notebook relies on.

1 · What is multi-omics?

DNAgenome · genomics
transcription →
mRNAwhich genes are used · transcriptomics
translation →
Proteinthe working molecules · proteomics
→
Phenotypetumour type, behaviour, outcome

miRNA small RNAs that bind mRNAs and silence them (reduce translation or stability). Green = layers measured in this project.

Omics
Measure all molecules of one kind at once: about 20,000 genes, about 2,000 miRNAs, hundreds of proteins.
Multi-omics
Several layers measured on the same samples. The questions: do the layers agree, and does combining them help?

2 · The data: TCGA breast cancer

LayerMeasured byUnit in the file
mRNARNA-seq (STAR counts)raw counts
miRNAsmall-RNA-seqlog2(RPM + 1)
ProteinRPPA (antibodies)normalised, centred
Clinicalpathology recordstext
Two designs in one data set
Matched pairs: 112 patients with tumour and normal tissue (Notebook 2).
Multi-omics tumours: 854 tumours with all three layers (Notebooks 3 and 4).
Read a TCGA barcode
TCGA-A7-A0CE-11A
TCGA-A7-A0CE = the patient
01 = primary tumour, 11 = normal tissue
Different units
Each layer arrives at a different stage of processing. Never combine them before bringing each one to a comparable scale.

3 · Breast cancer is several diseases: PAM50 subtypes

SubtypeBiologyTypical treatment
Luminal AER+, slow-growing, best prognosishormone therapy
Luminal BER+, faster-dividinghormone therapy ± chemotherapy
HER2-enrichedERBB2 (HER2) gene amplifiedanti-HER2 (trastuzumab)
Basal-likeER−/PR−/HER2− (“triple negative”), aggressivechemotherapy
Normal-likeresembles normal breast; small group, unclear—
PAM50
The subtype is assigned from the mRNA of 50 genes. Remember this: it matters for the machine learning.
ER status by IHC
A pathologist stains the tumour slide for the estrogen-receptor protein. This is a different measurement.

4 · Quality control: trust the data before you analyse it

CheckBad sign
Library sizetoo few reads → noisy
Genes detectedtoo few → failed library
% mitochondrial readsvery high → stressed cells or degraded RNA
Sex check (Y genes)disagrees with the record → sample swap
Sample correlation / PCAfar from its group → outlier
Missing valuesmany, in a pattern → batch or panel effect
Flag ≠ remove
A flag is a question. Remove a sample only for a reason you can state, and record it.
The decision log
For every QC decision: rule · how many · action. Anyone can then reproduce or challenge it.
One marker is not enough
A single Y gene can mislead (Notebook 1 shows this). Use several genes that agree.

5 · Normalisation, filtering and the log2 fold change

From counts to comparable numbers

1. CPM = count ÷ library size × 106. This removes sequencing depth.

2. log2(CPM + 1) removes the extreme skew; the +1 avoids log(0).

3. Filter: keep genes with CPM ≥ 1 in enough samples. Silent genes only add noise and extra tests.

log2 fold change (log2FC)
The difference on the log2 scale:
+12× higher
−1half
+38× higher
+664× higher
log2FC = 3 means about eight times more of this mRNA in the tumour.

6 · Differential expression: test every gene, then correct

Paired t-test
For each patient: tumour minus the same patient's normal. Is the average difference larger than its patient-to-patient spread allows by chance? Pairing removes age, genetics and ancestry.
p-value
How surprising the data would be if the gene did not change. With about 14,000 genes, 5 % ≈ 700 genes pass p < 0.05 by luck: these are false positives.
False Discovery Rate (Benjamini–Hochberg)
FDR < 0.05: about 5 % of the genes on the list are expected to be false positives.
Significant ≠ important
With many samples, tiny changes become “significant”. Also require a size: |log2FC| > 1 (at least 2-fold).

7 · Count models: what DESeq2 adds to the t-test

Counts, not logs
RNA-seq gives whole-number counts. DESeq2 models them with a negative binomial distribution: variance = mean + α·mean², where α (the dispersion) is the gene's biological noise.
Depth: median-of-ratios
Each sample's depth is the median over genes of its count divided by a reference sample. Genes that really change cannot distort it; the library total used by CPM can be distorted.
Pairing as a design formula
~ patient + tissue: one baseline per patient, then the tumour effect is estimated within patients. The last term is the one tested (Wald test, then BH).
Borrowing across genes
Genes with similar expression have similar noise, so each gene's dispersion is pulled towards a trend fitted over all genes.
When does the method matter?
With 3–5 samples per group: a lot. With 111 pairs each gene's variance is already well estimated, so here the count model is mainly a check.

8 · How to read a volcano plot

Two axes, two questions
x: how big is the change, and in which direction?
y: how sure are we?
Interesting genes
Upper corners only: a large fold change and a small FDR.
Big but low
A large fold change that is not significant is too noisy to trust; it may be a false negative.

9 · Bulk tissue is a mixture of cells

What a tissue sample contains
Cancer cells, fibroblasts (stroma), fat cells, immune cells, blood vessels and normal ducts, all ground up together. The RNA-seq signal is the weighted sum of all of them.
Normal breast
Mostly fat (adipocytes) with a few ducts lined by luminal and myoepithelial cells.
Composition, not regulation
A gene can look “down in cancer” simply because the tumour piece contains fewer of the cells that make it.
Correlation ≠ mechanism
Two molecules made by the same cell type rise and fall together across tumours, even if one does not control the other.
Take-home
Bulk omics tells us what changed in the tissue, not always in which cell.

10 · Integrating omics layers

StrategyIdea
Earlystandardise each layer, put them side by side, fit one model (used here)
Intermediatefind shared hidden factors (MOFA, DIABLO / mixOmics)
Lateone model per layer, then combine their predictions
Before combining
1. Same samples, in the same order, in every table.
2. Standardise each feature (mean 0, SD 1).
3. Weight each block by 1/√(number of features) so 2,000 genes do not drown 341 miRNAs.
Agreement between layers
Pearson correlation of the same gene's mRNA and protein across tumours. A miRNA and its target should correlate negatively.

11 · Machine-learning workflow

X, ysamples × features, labels
→
Split once75 % train / 25 % test (locked)
→
5-fold CVon the training set: compare models
→
Fitbest model on all training data
→
Test oncereport + interpret
Pipeline
scale → select 200 features → logistic regression. All of it inside cross-validation.
Metrics
Balanced accuracy: mean per-class accuracy (chance = 0.25 for 4 classes). Also the confusion matrix and ROC / AUC.
Regularisation
Features ≫ samples, so the weights are shrunk (C = 0.05) and the model cannot memorise noise.

12 · Two traps in omics machine learning

Data leakage
Choosing the “best” genes using all samples and then cross-validating lets the test samples influence the model. With thousands of genes this gives high accuracy even on random labels.

Rule: every step that looks at the labels goes inside cross-validation; the test set is touched once.
Circular labels
PAM50 subtypes were defined from mRNA. Predicting them from mRNA partly re-discovers the definition.

Remedy: also test a label measured independently, here ER status judged by a pathologist (IHC).
Take-home
A model is only as good as its labels and its validation.

Loading omics data, quality control (QC) and preprocessing

The project. We use real data from The Cancer Genome Atlas breast cancer study (TCGA-BRCA), downloaded from the UCSC Xena browser (GDC data hub). For the same patients we have three omics layers:

Layer What is measured File Unit
Transcriptome (mRNA) how many RNA-seq reads came from each gene mrna_counts.csv.gz raw read counts
miRNA small regulatory RNAs mirna_log2rpm.csv.gz log2(reads per million + 1)
Proteome ~490 proteins measured with antibodies (RPPA) protein_rppa.csv.gz normalised, centred values
Clinical sample type, PAM50 subtype, ER/PR/HER2 status, age, stage clinical_samples.csv text / numbers
Gene annotation Ensembl ID → gene symbol, chromosome gene_annotation.csv text

The four notebooks

  1. This one – load, understand, quality-check and clean every layer → save clean tables
  2. Differential expression: tumour vs matched normal tissue, volcano plots (mRNA and miRNA)
  3. Multi-omics integration: do the layers agree? (mRNA ↔ protein, miRNA ↔ mRNA, PCA)
  4. Machine learning: predict the breast-cancer subtype from each layer and from all layers together

Files needed (Colab): the five files in the data/ folder.

Step 1 · Load the five files

pd.read_csv reads .csv and also compressed .csv.gz files directly. index_col=0 makes the first column (gene / sample IDs) the row labels.

clin    = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/data/clinical_samples.csv', index_col=0)
genes   = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/data/gene_annotation.csv', index_col=0)
counts  = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/data/mrna_counts.csv.gz', index_col=0)
mirna   = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/data/mirna_log2rpm.csv.gz', index_col=0)
protein = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/data/protein_rppa.csv.gz', index_col=0)

for name, table in [('clinical', clin), ('gene annotation', genes), ('mRNA counts', counts),
                    ('miRNA', mirna), ('protein', protein)]:
    print(f'{name:16s} {table.shape[0]:6,d} rows  x {table.shape[1]:4d} columns')

Interpretation
  • Omics tables are wide: one row per feature (gene, miRNA, protein) and one column per sample. The mRNA table has 19,944 protein-coding genes × 975 samples – about 19.4 million numbers. Machine learning later needs the opposite shape (samples as rows), so we will transpose (.T).
  • The three layers arrive at different stages of processing: mRNA = raw integer counts (we must normalise them), miRNA = already log2(RPM+1), protein = already normalised and centred around 0 (negative values are normal here). Never mix layers before bringing each one to a comparable scale.
  • The protein table already shows NaN = missing values; we will have to deal with them.

Step 3 · The clinical labels we will predict and explain

PAM50 subtypes are the molecular "families" of breast cancer, defined from the expression of 50 genes:

Subtype Biology in one line Typical treatment
Luminal A ER+, slow-growing, best prognosis hormone therapy
Luminal B ER+, faster-growing (more proliferation) hormone therapy ± chemo
HER2-enriched ERBB2 (HER2) gene amplified anti-HER2 drugs (trastuzumab)
Basal-like ER–/PR–/HER2– ("triple negative"), aggressive chemotherapy
Normal-like looks like normal breast; small, unclear group –

ER status (IHC) is measured differently: a pathologist stains the tumour slide for the estrogen receptor protein.

Interpretation
  • The classes are unbalanced: Luminal A is the biggest group (326) and HER2-enriched the smallest (59). A model that always answers "LumA" would already be right about half the time, so in Notebook 4 we report balanced accuracy (the average of the per-class accuracies), not just accuracy.
  • 184 multi-omics tumours have no PAM50 label (missing in the source). We keep them aside and, as a bonus, let the final model predict their subtype.
  • The "Normal-like" group is small (16) and biologically unclear (often tumours with much normal tissue mixed in), so we will leave it out of the classification task.
  • Median age is 58 years – typical for breast cancer.

Count tables use stable Ensembl IDs (ENSG00000141736.14; the .14 is the version). People talk in gene symbols (ERBB2). The annotation file links the two – an everyday omics task.

Step 5 · mRNA quality control, sample by sample

Three classic RNA-seq QC numbers per sample:

Metric How Bad sign
Library size total reads = column sum very few reads → noisy
Genes detected genes with ≥ 1 read too few → degraded RNA / failed library
% mitochondrial reads reads from the 13 chrM genes very high → stressed / dying cells or degraded RNA 
lib_size = counts.sum()                         # column sums = reads per sample
detected = (counts > 0).sum()                   # genes with at least one read
is_mito  = genes['chrom'] == 'chrM'
pct_mito = counts[is_mito].sum() / lib_size * 100

qc = pd.DataFrame({'lib_size_M': lib_size / 1e6,
                   'genes_detected': detected,
                   'pct_mito': pct_mito,
                   'sample_type': clin.loc[counts.columns, 'sample_type']})
qc.describe().round(1)

Interpretation
  • Library sizes run from 18.9 to 110.9 million reads (median 55.7 M): every sample is well above a common 10 M minimum. Genes detected: 15,971–19,065 of 19,944, so no failed library.
  • 4 tumours have more than 20 % mitochondrial reads (up to 40.6 %). That is a flag, not a verdict: tumours can be rich in mitochondria. We keep them but check below whether they look abnormal compared with other samples (correlation and PCA). Removing data needs a reason; flagging costs nothing.
  • The dashed lines are rules of thumb – each lab sets its own cut-offs and must report them.

Step 6 · Sex check: does the data agree with the clinical record?

Breast cancer also occurs in men (about 1 %). Genes on the Y chromosome are expressed only in male cells, so their expression must match the recorded gender. A mismatch reveals a sample swap or labelling error – one of the most valuable QC checks there is.

First we need comparable numbers: CPM (counts per million) = count ÷ library size × 1,000,000, then log2(CPM + 1).

cpm    = counts / lib_size * 1e6           # each column divided by its own library size
logcpm = np.log2(cpm + 1)

y_genes = ['RPS4Y1', 'DDX3Y', 'KDM5D', 'UTY']
ychr = logcpm.loc[symbol[symbol.isin(y_genes)].index]
ychr.index = symbol[ychr.index]            # show symbols instead of Ensembl IDs
gender = clin.loc[counts.columns, 'gender']

for g in y_genes:
    print(f'{g:7s} expressed (log2CPM > 2):', pd.crosstab(gender, ychr.loc[g] > 2).to_dict())
Output

qc['gender'] = gender

  • All 10 samples recorded as male express the Y genes; no female sample expresses DDX3Y, KDM5D or UTY. Combined Y score → 0 mismatches: the clinical labels are trustworthy.
  • But look at RPS4Y1 alone: it would have flagged 3 women as "male". Their RPS4Y1 is only modestly raised while the other three Y genes are ~0 – most likely reads from the very similar X-chromosome copy RPS4X being mis-assigned. Lesson: never trust a single marker; use several genes that agree.

Step 7 · Why we normalise and log-transform

Raw counts depend on sequencing depth (a sample with twice the reads has ~twice the counts for every gene) and are extremely skewed (a few genes have millions of reads, most have tens). We fix depth with CPM and skew with log2.

some = counts.columns[:24]                 # 24 samples, enough to see the pattern
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.8))
axes[0].boxplot(counts[some].values, showfliers=False); axes[0].set_title('1. Raw counts')
axes[1].boxplot(cpm[some].values, showfliers=False);    axes[1].set_title('2. CPM (depth corrected)')
axes[2].boxplot(logcpm[some].values, showfliers=False); axes[2].set_title('3. log2(CPM + 1)')
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_xlabel('24 samples')
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('01_normalisation_boxplots'); plt.show()
Output
Interpretation
  • Raw counts: boxes sit at different heights because samples were sequenced to different depths, and the scale is dominated by a few huge values (outliers hidden here).
  • CPM: boxes line up – depth differences are removed – but the data are still squashed near zero.
  • log2(CPM + 1): symmetric, comparable boxes. A difference of 1 on this scale = a 2-fold change, which is why fold changes in omics are reported as log2 fold change. The "+1" avoids log(0).

Step 8 · Remove genes that are barely expressed

A gene with 0–2 reads in most samples carries no information and only adds noise (and multiple-testing burden). Rule used here: keep a gene if CPM ≥ 1 in at least half of the samples.

keep_gene = (cpm >= 1).mean(axis=1) >= 0.5          # fraction of samples with CPM >= 1
print('Genes kept:', keep_gene.sum(), 'of', len(keep_gene))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), sharey=True)
for s in counts.columns[:12]:
    sns.kdeplot(logcpm[s], ax=axes[0], lw=0.8, legend=False)
    sns.kdeplot(logcpm.loc[keep_gene, s], ax=axes[1], lw=0.8, legend=False)
axes[0].set_title('All genes'); axes[1].set_title('After filtering')
for ax in axes: ax.set_xlabel('log2(CPM + 1)')
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('01_filtering_density'); plt.show()
Output
Genes kept: 13536 of 19944
Interpretation
  • 13,536 of 19,944 protein-coding genes pass the filter (68 %). The others are mostly tissue-specific genes switched off in breast (e.g. brain, testis, olfactory receptors).
  • Left plot: a tall spike at 0 (silent genes). Right plot: the spike is gone and every sample shows one smooth hump – the expressed genes we can analyse.

Step 9 · Look at all samples at once: PCA and sample correlation

PCA (principal component analysis) squeezes ~13,000 genes into a few new axes that capture the biggest differences between samples. Samples close together have similar expression profiles. We use the 2,000 most variable genes.

Outlier check: for every sample, its median correlation with the other samples of the same type. A sample far below the rest is suspicious.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

expr = logcpm[keep_gene]
top_var = expr.var(axis=1).nlargest(2000).index
X = expr.loc[top_var].T                       # samples as rows for PCA
X = X - X.mean()                              # centre each gene

pca = PCA(n_components=5)
pcs = pca.fit_transform(X)
qc['PC1'], qc['PC2'] = pcs[:, 0], pcs[:, 1]
print('Variance explained by PC1-PC5 (%):', (pca.explained_variance_ratio_ * 100).round(1))
Output
Variance explained by PC1-PC5 (%): [17.8 13.7  5.5  4.5  3.2]
med_corr = pd.Series(index=expr.columns, dtype=float)
cutoff = {}
for t in ['Tumour', 'Normal']:
    cols = qc.index[qc.sample_type == t]
    c = np.corrcoef(expr[cols].T.values)          # sample-by-sample correlation
    np.fill_diagonal(c, np.nan)
    med_corr[cols] = np.nanmedian(c, axis=1)
    q1, q3 = med_corr[cols].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    cutoff[t] = q1 - 3 * (q3 - q1)                # far below the box: a strict outlier rule
qc['median_corr'] = med_corr
qc['flag_outlier'] = qc['median_corr'] < qc['sample_type'].map(cutoff)
print('Outlier cut-offs:', {t: round(v, 3) for t, v in cutoff.items()})
qc[qc['flag_outlier'] | qc['flag_high_mito']][['sample_type', 'median_corr', 'pct_mito']].round(3)
Output
Outlier cut-offs: {'Tumour': 0.66, 'Normal': 0.797}
sample_type median_corr pct_mito
TCGA-AO-A0J9-01A Tumour 0.827 22.464
TCGA-AO-A0JB-01A Tumour 0.791 40.626
TCGA-AO-A0JL-01A Tumour 0.756 23.846
TCGA-E2-A1LS-01A Tumour 0.745 28.977
TCGA-GI-A2C8-11A Normal 0.717 10.561 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
for t in ['Tumour', 'Normal']:
    d = qc[qc.sample_type == t]
    ax.scatter(d.PC1, d.PC2, s=10, alpha=0.6, color=COLORS[t], label=t)
for flag, mark, lab in [('flag_high_mito', 's', '>20 % mito'), ('flag_outlier', 'X', 'correlation outlier')]:
    d = qc[qc[flag]]
    ax.scatter(d.PC1, d.PC2, s=90, facecolors='none' if mark == 's' else 'black', edgecolors='black', marker=mark, label=lab)
ax.set_xlabel(f'PC1 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]*100:.1f} %)')
ax.set_ylabel(f'PC2 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]*100:.1f} %)')
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('01_pca_samples'); plt.show()

# Which tumours are where? (a first look at biology in the QC plot)
t = qc[qc.sample_type == 'Tumour'].join(clin['pam50_subtype'])
print('Median PC1  all tumours:', round(t.PC1.median(), 1),
      '| PAM50 Normal-like tumours:', round(t.loc[t.pam50_subtype == 'Normal', 'PC1'].median(), 1))
low = t[t.PC2 < -30]
print('Tumours in the lower group (PC2 < -30):', len(low), low.pam50_subtype.value_counts(dropna=False).to_dict())
Output
Median PC1  all tumours: -9.1 | PAM50 Normal-like tumours: 26.8
Tumours in the lower group (PC2 < -30): 161 {'Basal': 113, nan: 38, 'Her2': 9, 'Normal': 1}
Interpretation
  • PC1 (17.8 % of the variation) separates normal tissue from tumours – the largest signal in the whole data set is the biology we care about, not a technical artefact. Good news.
  • Tumours spread much more widely than normals: tumours are heterogeneous (different subtypes), normal breast is similar from person to person.
  • The four high-mito tumours (squares) sit inside the tumour cloud and correlate normally with other tumours → kept.
  • One sample, TCGA-GI-A2C8-11A (a normal sample, black X), correlates poorly with the other normals (median r = 0.717; cut-off 0.797; most normals ≈ 0.93) and sits half-way between the normal and the tumour cloud. The likeliest explanation: tumour cells inside the "normal" tissue piece. → removed. Because it is the normal half of a matched pair, its tumour partner also leaves the paired analysis; 111 pairs remain.
  • The reverse also happens: tumours labelled PAM50 Normal-like sit at a median PC1 of 26.8 versus -9.1 for all tumours – tumour samples with a lot of normal breast tissue mixed in.
  • PC2 splits the tumours into two groups. The lower group (161 tumours) contains 113 of the 115 Basal-like tumours: Basal-like breast cancer is so different from the others that it shows up even in a QC plot made without any labels. We will meet this again in Notebooks 3 and 4.

Step 10 · miRNA quality control

The miRNA file lists all 1,881 human miRNAs in miRBase, but any one tissue expresses only a few hundred.

print('Fraction of zero values in the miRNA table:', round((mirna == 0).mean().mean(), 3))
keep_mirna = (mirna >= 1).mean(axis=1) >= 0.5          # log2(RPM+1) >= 1  means RPM >= 1
print('miRNAs expressed (RPM >= 1 in half the samples):', keep_mirna.sum(), 'of', len(keep_mirna))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.4))
ax.hist(mirna.mean(axis=1), bins=60, color='grey', edgecolor='white')
ax.axvline(1, color='black', ls='--'); ax.set_yscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel('Mean log2(RPM + 1) across samples'); ax.set_ylabel('Number of miRNAs (log scale)')
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('01_mirna_expression'); plt.show()
print(mirna.mean(axis=1).nlargest(5).round(1))

Step 11 · Protein quality control: missing values

RPPA measures each protein with a specific antibody. Antibodies were added and retired over the years, so some proteins were not measured on all slides.

miss_by_protein = protein.isna().mean(axis=1) * 100       # % missing for each protein
miss_by_sample  = protein.isna().mean(axis=0) * 100       # % missing for each sample

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.6))
axes[0].hist(miss_by_protein, bins=50, color='grey', edgecolor='white'); axes[0].set_yscale('log')
axes[0].axvline(20, color='black', ls='--'); axes[0].set_xlabel('% missing per protein'); axes[0].set_ylabel('Proteins (log scale)')
axes[1].hist(miss_by_sample, bins=50, color='grey', edgecolor='white'); axes[1].set_yscale('log')
axes[1].axvline(50, color='black', ls='--'); axes[1].set_xlabel('% missing per sample'); axes[1].set_ylabel('Samples (log scale)')
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('01_protein_missing'); plt.show()

print('Proteins with > 20 % missing:', (miss_by_protein > 20).sum())
print('Samples with > 50 % missing:', (miss_by_sample > 50).sum())
print(miss_by_sample.round(1).value_counts().head(4))
Output

Samples with > 50 % missing: 18
4.7    400
4.9    304
6.0     73

Name: count, dtype: int64
good_proteins = miss_by_protein <= 20
good_samples  = miss_by_sample <= 50
prot = protein.loc[good_proteins, good_samples]

# remaining gaps: fill each protein with its own median (simple, robust imputation)
print('Missing values left before imputation:', int(prot.isna().sum().sum()))
prot = prot.apply(lambda row: row.fillna(row.median()), axis=1)
print('Missing values after imputation:', int(prot.isna().sum().sum()), '| table:', prot.shape)
Output
Missing values left before imputation: 792
Missing values after imputation: 0 | table: (463, 836)
Interpretation
  • Missingness is structured, not random: 24 proteins are missing in more than 20 % of samples (antibodies used only in some batches), and 18 samples miss 54 % of all proteins – they were run on a smaller antibody panel. Filling half a sample with made-up values would be fiction, so these samples and proteins are removed.
  • The few remaining gaps (792 values, 0.2 % of the table) are filled with the protein's median. Median imputation is simple and does not invent extreme values, but it slightly shrinks variation – fine for a few %, wrong for 50 %.
  • Final protein table: 463 proteins × 836 tumours.

Step 12 · Build the final multi-omics cohort and save clean tables

A tumour enters the multi-omics cohort only if it passed QC in every layer. For mRNA we re-apply the expression filter on these tumours only and switch to gene symbols.

qc['remove'] = qc['flag_low_lib'] | qc['flag_few_genes'] | qc['flag_outlier'] | qc['sex_mismatch']
mrna_ok = qc.index[~qc['remove']]

final = [s for s in clin.index[clin['in_multiomics']]
         if s in mrna_ok and s in prot.columns and s in mirna.columns]
print('Multi-omics tumours passing all QC:', len(final))

# mRNA: tumours only, expressed genes, one row per gene symbol
m = logcpm[final]
m = m[(cpm[final] >= 1).mean(axis=1) >= 0.5]
m.index = symbol[m.index]
m = m[~m.index.duplicated(keep='first')]
mirna_final = mirna.loc[keep_mirna, final]
prot_final = prot[final]

m.round(3).to_csv(f'{ROOT}/processed/mrna_logcpm_tumours.csv.gz')
mirna_final.round(3).to_csv(f'{ROOT}/processed/mirna_tumours.csv.gz')
prot_final.round(4).to_csv(f'{ROOT}/processed/protein_tumours.csv.gz')

samples_qc = clin.join(qc.drop(columns=['sample_type', 'gender']))
samples_qc['in_final_multiomics'] = samples_qc.index.isin(final)
samples_qc.to_csv(f'{ROOT}/processed/samples_qc.csv')
for f in ['mrna_logcpm_tumours.csv.gz', 'mirna_tumours.csv.gz', 'protein_tumours.csv.gz', 'samples_qc.csv']:
    print(f'saved processed/{f}')
print('mRNA', m.shape, '| miRNA', mirna_final.shape, '| protein', prot_final.shape)

NOTEBOOK 2 OF 4

Differential expression: tumour vs own normal

Executed notebook CII_02_Differential_Expression_Volcano_INSTRUCTOR.ipynb: code, real output, figures and interpretation.

Differential expression: tumour vs the patient's own normal tissue

Question: which genes (and miRNAs) change when normal breast tissue becomes a tumour?

Design: 111 patients gave a tumour and a normal sample. For every gene we compare each tumour with its own normal (a paired comparison), then correct for testing ~13,000 genes at once, and draw the result as a volcano plot. Finally we check the answer with a proper count model (PyDESeq2, paired design) and see whether the conclusions hold.

Files needed (Colab): mrna_counts.csv.gz, gene_annotation.csv, mirna_log2rpm.csv.gz (from data/) and samples_qc.csv (from processed/, made by Notebook 1).

Setup cell: Google Colab file upload (does nothing on your own computer)
# ▶ Google Colab only: upload the files listed above (you can select them all at once).
# On your own computer (Jupyter / VS Code) this cell does nothing - the files are already in the folders.

try:
    from google.colab import files
    RAW = ['clinical_samples.csv', 'gene_annotation.csv', 'mrna_counts.csv.gz', 'mirna_log2rpm.csv.gz', 'protein_rppa.csv.gz']
    for name in files.upload():
        folder = 'data' if name in RAW else 'processed'
        os.makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)
        os.replace(name, f'{folder}/{name}')
except ImportError:
    print('Not on Colab: using the local data/ and processed/ folders')

def save_fig(name):

from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
Output
Working folder: /Users/avinashgopa/PyBio10/Capstone_II_Multiomics

Step 1 · Build the matched pairs

We use the QC table from Notebook 1, drop the outlier sample, and keep only patients who still have both samples. Tumours and normals are sorted by patient so that column i of each list is the same person.

samples = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/processed/samples_qc.csv', index_col=0)
genes   = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/data/gene_annotation.csv', index_col=0)
counts  = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/data/mrna_counts.csv.gz', index_col=0)

pairs = samples[samples['in_DE_pairs'] & ~samples['flag_outlier']]
both = pairs['patient_id'].value_counts()
both = both[both == 2].index                                  # patients with tumour AND normal

T = pairs[(pairs.sample_type == 'Tumour') & pairs.patient_id.isin(both)].sort_values('patient_id')
N = pairs[(pairs.sample_type == 'Normal') & pairs.patient_id.isin(both)].sort_values('patient_id')
print('Same patient order in both lists?', (T.patient_id.values == N.patient_id.values).all())

tumour_ids, normal_ids = T.index.tolist(), N.index.tolist()
print('Matched pairs:', len(tumour_ids))
print(pd.DataFrame({'tumour': tumour_ids[:3], 'normal': normal_ids[:3]}))
Output
Same patient order in both lists? True
Matched pairs: 111
             tumour            normal
0  TCGA-A7-A0CE-01A  TCGA-A7-A0CE-11A
1  TCGA-A7-A0CH-01A  TCGA-A7-A0CH-11A
2  TCGA-A7-A0D9-01A  TCGA-A7-A0D9-11A

Step 2 · Normalise and filter for this comparison

Same recipe as Notebook 1 (CPM → log2), but the filter now asks: is the gene expressed (CPM ≥ 1) in at least as many samples as one group has? That keeps genes switched on only in tumours or only in normals – exactly the genes we are looking for.

sub = counts[tumour_ids + normal_ids]
cpm = sub / sub.sum() * 1e6
keep = (cpm >= 1).sum(axis=1) >= len(tumour_ids)
logcpm = np.log2(cpm[keep] + 1)
symbol = genes.loc[logcpm.index, 'gene_symbol']
print('Genes tested:', keep.sum(), 'of', len(keep))
Output
Genes tested: 13774 of 19944

Step 3 · Fold change and a paired t-test for every gene

  • log2 fold change (log2FC) = mean over patients of (tumour − own normal) on the log2 scale. +1 = twice as high in tumour, −1 = half, +3 = 8 times.
  • Paired t-test asks: is the average tumour-minus-normal difference larger than expected by chance, given how much it varies between patients? stats.ttest_rel(..., axis=1) runs it for all genes at once (one test per row).
tum_vals  = logcpm[tumour_ids].values
norm_vals = logcpm[normal_ids].values

log2fc = (tum_vals - norm_vals).mean(axis=1)                     # paired difference, averaged
t_stat, p_val = stats.ttest_rel(tum_vals, norm_vals, axis=1)     # one paired t-test per gene

de = pd.DataFrame({'symbol': symbol.values,
                   'mean_normal': norm_vals.mean(axis=1),
                   'mean_tumour': tum_vals.mean(axis=1),
                   'log2FC': log2fc, 't': t_stat, 'p_value': p_val}, index=logcpm.index)
de.head()

ax.hist(de['p_value'], bins=50, color='grey', edgecolor='white')
ax.set_xlabel('p-value'); ax.set_ylabel('Number of genes')

print('Genes with p < 0.05:', (de.p_value < 0.05).sum(), 'of', len(de))
Output
Genes with p < 0.05: 10805 of 13774
Interpretation
  • If no gene changed, p-values would be spread evenly between 0 and 1 (flat histogram), and 5 % of genes (≈ 689 genes) would have p < 0.05 purely by chance – false positives.
  • Here we see a huge spike near 0: 10,805 genes (78 %) have p < 0.05. Tumour and normal breast differ in thousands of genes. That is real biology, but the chance hits are mixed in, so we need a correction (next step).

Step 4 · Multiple testing: from p-values to the False Discovery Rate (FDR)

Testing ~13,000 genes at p < 0.05 guarantees hundreds of false positives. The Benjamini–Hochberg FDR controls the fraction of false discoveries among the genes we call significant: FDR < 0.05 means "about 5 % of this list may be false positives".

Statistical significance is not enough: with 111 pairs even tiny changes become "significant". We also ask for a biologically meaningful size: |log2FC| > 1 (at least 2-fold).

de['FDR'] = multipletests(de['p_value'], method='fdr_bh')[1]

up   = (de.FDR < 0.05) & (de.log2FC > 1)
down = (de.FDR < 0.05) & (de.log2FC < -1)
de['call'] = np.select([up, down], ['Up in tumour', 'Down in tumour'], default='Not significant')

steps = pd.Series({'p < 0.05': (de.p_value < 0.05).sum(),
                   'FDR < 0.05': (de.FDR < 0.05).sum(),
                   'FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1': (up | down).sum(),
                   '   of which up in tumour': up.sum(),
                   '   of which down in tumour': down.sum()}, name='genes')
steps.to_frame()
Output
genes
p < 0.05 10805
FDR < 0.05 10655
FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1 2224
of which up in tumour 690
of which down in tumour 1534
Interpretation
  • FDR correction barely shrinks the list (10,805 → 10,655) because the signal is so strong; in weaker experiments it removes most hits.
  • The effect-size filter does the real work: only 2,224 genes change at least 2-fold – 690 up and 1,534 down. With many samples, "significant" ≠ "important": always report both the FDR and the fold change.

Step 5 · The volcano plot

Each dot is a gene. x = log2 fold change (left = lower in tumour, right = higher), y = −log10(FDR) (higher = more confident). Interesting genes sit in the upper corners: big change and strong evidence.

de['minus_log10_fdr'] = -np.log10(de['FDR'])
colors = {'Up in tumour': '#c0392b', 'Down in tumour': '#2e86c1', 'Not significant': 'lightgrey'}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
for call, col in colors.items():
    d = de[de.call == call]
    ax.scatter(d.log2FC, d.minus_log10_fdr, s=6, color=col, alpha=0.7, label=f'{call} ({len(d)})')
ax.axvline(1, color='black', ls='--', lw=0.8); ax.axvline(-1, color='black', ls='--', lw=0.8)
ax.axhline(-np.log10(0.05), color='black', ls='--', lw=0.8)

def add_labels(ax, d, x, y, name, side, gap):
    # write names next to points, pushing labels apart vertically so they do not overlap
    last = -np.inf
    for _, r in d.sort_values(y).iterrows():
        ty = max(r[y], last + gap)
        tx = r[x] + (0.4 if side == 'right' else -0.4)
        ax.annotate(r[name], (r[x], r[y]), xytext=(tx, ty), fontsize=7.5, ha='left' if side == 'right' else 'right',
                    va='center', arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='-', lw=0.4, color='grey'))
        last = ty

add_labels(ax, de[up].nlargest(10, 'log2FC'), 'log2FC', 'minus_log10_fdr', 'symbol', 'right', gap=2.6)
add_labels(ax, de[down].nsmallest(10, 'log2FC'), 'log2FC', 'minus_log10_fdr', 'symbol', 'left', gap=2.6)
ax.set_xlim(-8, 8)
ax.set_xlabel('log2 fold change (tumour vs own normal)'); ax.set_ylabel('-log10(FDR)')
ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=8, frameon=True)
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('02_volcano_mrna'); plt.show()
Output

print('\nTop 12 DOWN in tumour')
print(de[down].nsmallest(12, 'log2FC')[cols].round(2).to_string(index=False, formatters={'FDR': '{:.1e}'.format}))

Interpretation

The volcano is lopsided: more genes go down (1,534) than up (690), and the down-genes form a tall left arm. Reading the gene names tells the biology:

  • Up – remodelling of the tissue around the tumour (stroma): COL10A1 (log2FC 6.09, ≈ 68-fold), MMP11 (5.72), COL11A1 (5.32), COMP, INHBA, LRRC15. These are made by cancer-associated fibroblasts that build a stiff, collagen-rich matrix and digest the old one (MMPs). COL11A1 and COL10A1 are among the most consistent tumour-vs-normal markers across many cancers.
  • Up – cell division: TOP2A (3.53), MKI67 (3.16), NEK2, RRM2, TPX2, KIF4A – tumours proliferate. (TOP2A is the target of anthracycline chemotherapy; Ki-67 is the pathologist's proliferation stain.)
  • Down – fat cells: FABP4 (-5.58), LEP (leptin, -5.42), ADIPOQ (adiponectin, -5.24), PLIN1, CIDEC, GPD1. Normal breast is mostly adipose tissue; a tumour sample contains far fewer fat cells. These genes are not "switched off by cancer" – the cell mixture changed.

Key lesson: bulk RNA-seq measures a mixture of cell types, so many "DE genes" reflect tissue composition, not gene regulation inside cancer cells.

Step 6 · MA plot and individual genes

The MA plot shows fold change against average expression: it reveals whether only lowly expressed (noisy) genes change. Then we look at the raw story behind four genes: one line per patient from normal to tumour.

de['mean_expr'] = (de.mean_normal + de.mean_tumour) / 2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.2))
for call, col in colors.items():
    d = de[de.call == call]
    ax.scatter(d.mean_expr, d.log2FC, s=5, color=col, alpha=0.6, label=call)
ax.axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('Average expression, log2(CPM + 1)'); ax.set_ylabel('log2 fold change'); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('02_MA_plot'); plt.show()

Step 7 · Heatmap of the top genes

The 25 strongest up and 25 strongest down genes, each row scaled to mean 0 and SD 1 (a z-score) so that colours compare samples, not genes. Samples are clustered without being told which is tumour or normal.

Interpretation
  • Without using labels, the two main sample clusters are almost pure: all 111 normals in one, and only 6 of 111 tumours join them – most likely tumour pieces with little tumour content, the same kind of samples we saw near the normals in the PCA of Notebook 1. 50 genes are enough to tell the tissues apart.

Step 8 · From gene lists to biology: a simple "theme" test

Instead of reading genes one by one, we collect marker genes for four well-known processes (lists curated from textbook markers; see the comment in the code) and ask whether the whole group shifts. The Mann–Whitney test compares the t-statistics of the group with all other genes – a mini gene-set enrichment test.

# Hand-curated marker lists (classic markers from textbooks and reviews; small on purpose)
themes = {
  'Cell cycle / proliferation': ['MKI67', 'TOP2A', 'CCNB1', 'CDK1', 'BIRC5', 'AURKA', 'BUB1', 'CENPF', 'KIF2C', 'MCM2',
                                 'PLK1', 'CCNA2', 'TPX2', 'UBE2C', 'CDC20', 'FOXM1', 'MYBL2', 'PTTG1', 'RRM2', 'NEK2'],
  'Matrix remodelling (fibroblasts)': ['COL1A1', 'COL1A2', 'COL3A1', 'COL5A1', 'COL10A1', 'COL11A1', 'FN1', 'POSTN',
                                 'MMP11', 'MMP13', 'MMP1', 'COMP', 'INHBA', 'LRRC15', 'SULF1', 'FAP', 'CTHRC1'],
  'Fat cells (adipocytes)': ['ADIPOQ', 'LEP', 'PLIN1', 'PLIN4', 'FABP4', 'CIDEA', 'CIDEC', 'LPL', 'CD36', 'PPARG',
                                 'LIPE', 'GPD1', 'PCK1', 'AQP7', 'RBP4', 'TRARG1'],
  'Myoepithelial / basal layer': ['KRT5', 'KRT14', 'KRT17', 'TP63', 'MYH11', 'OXTR', 'KIT', 'ACTG2', 'CNN1', 'MYLK'],
}
rows = []
for name, members in themes.items():
    in_set = de.symbol.isin(members)
    p = stats.mannwhitneyu(de.loc[in_set, 't'], de.loc[~in_set, 't']).pvalue
    rows.append([name, in_set.sum(), de.loc[in_set, 'log2FC'].median(), p])
theme_res = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['theme', 'genes found', 'median log2FC', 'Mann-Whitney p']).set_index('theme')
theme_res.round(2).style.format({'Mann-Whitney p': '{:.1e}'})

Interpretation
Theme median log2FC What it means

Every theme differs from the background (all p < 1e-6). In four lines we have turned 2,000 genes into a biological story. Real projects use thousands of curated gene sets (GO, KEGG, Reactome, MSigDB) with the same logic.

Step 9 · Did the pairing help?

Run the unpaired Welch t-test on exactly the same data and compare.

p_unpaired = stats.ttest_ind(tum_vals, norm_vals, axis=1, equal_var=False).pvalue
fdr_unpaired = multipletests(p_unpaired, method='fdr_bh')[1]
n_paired   = ((de.FDR < 0.05) & (de.log2FC.abs() > 1)).sum()
n_unpaired = ((fdr_unpaired < 0.05) & (de.log2FC.abs() > 1)).sum()
print('Significant 2-fold genes  paired:', n_paired, '| unpaired:', n_unpaired)
print('Median -log10(p)  paired:', round(np.median(-np.log10(de.p_value)), 2),
      '| unpaired:', round(np.median(-np.log10(p_unpaired)), 2))
Output
Significant 2-fold genes  paired: 2224 | unpaired: 2224
Median -log10(p)  paired: 5.8 | unpaired: 5.43
Interpretation
  • With 111 pairs and such large effects, both tests find the same number of 2-fold genes (2224 vs 2224).
  • But the evidence is stronger with pairing (median −log10 p 5.8 vs 5.4) because patient-to-patient differences are removed. With few samples (say 5 pairs) this gain often decides whether you find anything at all.

Step 10 · Check the answer with a count model: PyDESeq2 (paired design)

The paired t-test on log2(CPM + 1) is easy to understand, but it is an approximation. RNA-seq gives counts, and the standard tools (DESeq2, edgeR, limma-voom) model counts directly. Here we run PyDESeq2, the Python version of DESeq2, on the same raw counts, same genes, same 111 pairs, and ask: do our conclusions survive a proper count model?

Paired t-test (Steps 3–4) PyDESeq2
data log2(CPM + 1) raw integer counts, negative-binomial model
depth correction library size (CPM) median-of-ratios size factors, robust to genes that change
pairing tumour − own normal design formula ~ patient + tissue: one baseline per patient, then the tumour effect
noise per gene from this gene alone dispersion shared across genes (trend + shrinkage)
test paired t-test, BH Wald test, BH with independent filtering

~ patient + tissue is how a paired design is written in DESeq2: patient absorbs each person's own level (age, genetics, how the sample was handled), so tissue (Tumour vs Normal) is estimated within patients. The last term is the one we test.

The fit takes a few minutes (about 1 min on a laptop, about 3 min on Colab): 222 samples × ~13,000 genes, 112 coefficients per gene.

# PyDESeq2 = DESeq2 in Python. On Colab it is installed here (about 1 minute); on your computer: pip install pydeseq2
try:
    import pydeseq2
except ImportError:
    !pip install -q pydeseq2
    import pydeseq2
from pydeseq2.dds import DeseqDataSet
from pydeseq2.ds import DeseqStats
print('PyDESeq2 version', pydeseq2.__version__)
Output
PyDESeq2 version 0.6.0
import time
ids = tumour_ids + normal_ids
meta = pd.DataFrame({'patient': samples.loc[ids, 'patient_id'].str.replace('-', '_').values,   # '_' is safer in a formula
                     'tissue': ['Tumour'] * len(tumour_ids) + ['Normal'] * len(normal_ids)}, index=ids)
raw = sub.loc[logcpm.index]               # RAW counts of the same genes the t-test used
print('Raw counts are whole numbers:', bool((raw % 1 == 0).all().all()))
print(meta.head(3)); print(meta.tissue.value_counts().to_dict())

start = time.time()
dds = DeseqDataSet(counts=raw.T, metadata=meta, design='~patient + tissue', quiet=True)   # samples in ROWS, so .T
dds.deseq2()                                                       # size factors -> dispersions -> model fit
ds = DeseqStats(dds, contrast=['tissue', 'Tumour', 'Normal'], quiet=True)
ds.summary()                                                       # Wald test + BH
print(f'Fitted {raw.shape[0]:,} genes x {raw.shape[1]} samples in {(time.time() - start) / 60:.1f} min')

res = ds.results_df.copy()
res['symbol'] = de['symbol']
d_up   = (res.padj < 0.05) & (res.log2FoldChange > 1)
d_down = (res.padj < 0.05) & (res.log2FoldChange < -1)
pd.Series({'padj < 0.05': (res.padj < 0.05).sum(),
           'padj < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1': (d_up | d_down).sum(),

10a · Size factors: does library size tell the truth about depth?

DESeq2 estimates sequencing depth with the median-of-ratios: the median, over genes, of each sample's count divided by a reference (the geometric mean over all samples). The median ignores genes that really change. CPM uses the total, which the changed genes can push up or down. If the two disagree systematically between tumours and normals, every CPM-based fold change is shifted.

lib_ratio = sub.sum() / np.exp(np.log(sub.sum()).mean())          # library size on the same scale (geometric mean 1)
sf = dds.obs['size_factors']
depth = pd.DataFrame({'tissue': meta.tissue, 'libsize / size factor': lib_ratio[ids] / sf})
print(depth.groupby('tissue')['libsize / size factor'].describe()[['25%', '50%', '75%']].round(3))

shift = np.log2(depth.groupby('tissue')['libsize / size factor'].median())
print(f"Expected shift of CPM-based log2FC: {shift['Tumour'] - shift['Normal']:+.2f}")

common = de.index.intersection(res.index)
diff = res.loc[common, 'log2FoldChange'] - de.loc[common, 'log2FC']
print(f'Median (DESeq2 log2FC - t-test log2FC): {diff.median():+.2f}')
Output
          25%    50%    75%
tissue                     
Normal  0.891  0.945  1.069
Tumour  0.943  1.002  1.059
Expected shift of CPM-based log2FC: +0.08
Median (DESeq2 log2FC - t-test log2FC): +0.03
Interpretation
  • Library size ÷ size factor is 1.0 for a typical tumour and 0.95 for a typical normal: a difference of only +0.08 on the log2 scale (about 6 %). In this dataset the simple CPM correction is almost as good as the median-of-ratios, and the overall median difference between DESeq2 and t-test fold changes is just +0.03.
  • Biology: normal breast is mostly fat and tumours are mostly epithelial and stromal cells, so the risk of a composition bias was real. It turned out small here because no handful of genes dominates the reads. In experiments where a few genes take a large share of all reads (e.g. strong induction, blood samples with haemoglobin), it can be large, which is why count models use the median-of-ratios.

Output
Interpretation
  • PyDESeq2 keeps almost every t-test gene: 2,208 of the 2,224 (only 16 lost), and adds 529 more, giving 2,737 2-fold genes (889 up, 1,848 down). Fold changes agree closely (r = 0.975).
  • The added genes are borderline, not new biology: 94 % of all disagreements sit near the 2-fold line (|log2FC| 0.7–1.3) in one of the methods. For the added genes the median log2FC is -0.62 by the t-test but -1.06 by PyDESeq2, and 62 % of them are down in tumour. The top-100 lists (ranked by p-value) share 62 genes: with 111 pairs hundreds of genes have p-values near zero, so the exact order is unstable.
  • Why PyDESeq2 gives slightly larger fold changes: the +1 in log2(CPM + 1) pulls small values towards 0, which squeezes the fold change of weakly expressed genes. The gap is largest for weak genes (median |log2FC| larger by +0.11 when mean log2CPM < 4) and almost zero for strong ones (+0.03 above 4). A count model has no pseudo-count.
  • The landmark genes keep their direction and story, but genes that are almost absent in one tissue get larger fold changes from PyDESeq2: COL10A1 6.09 → 7.5, LEP -5.42 → -7.31, ADIPOQ -5.24 → -6.13, FABP4 -5.58 → -5.94 (t-test → PyDESeq2). Near zero CPM the +1 caps how far log2(CPM + 1) can fall, so the t-test under-states the biggest changes. Genes expressed in both tissues change little (TOP2A 3.53 → 3.73, MKI67 3.16 → 3.39).
  • Why so similar overall? With 111 pairs each gene's variance is already well estimated, so the t-test is a fair approximation. A count model matters most in small experiments (3–5 samples per group), where sharing information across genes changes the answer a lot. Here it serves as a sensitivity analysis: the conclusions do not depend on the method, only the exact length of the list near the cut-off does.

Step 11 · The same analysis for miRNAs

miRNA values are already log2(RPM + 1), so we skip the CPM step.

mirna = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/data/mirna_log2rpm.csv.gz', index_col=0)
ok = [(t, n) for t, n in zip(tumour_ids, normal_ids) if t in mirna.columns and n in mirna.columns]
mt = [t for t, n in ok]; mn = [n for t, n in ok]
print('Pairs with miRNA data:', len(ok))

mi = mirna[mt + mn]
mi = mi[(mi >= 1).sum(axis=1) >= len(ok)]
mde = pd.DataFrame({'log2FC': (mi[mt].values - mi[mn].values).mean(axis=1),
                    'p_value': stats.ttest_rel(mi[mt].values, mi[mn].values, axis=1).pvalue}, index=mi.index)
mde['FDR'] = multipletests(mde.p_value, method='fdr_bh')[1]
m_up = (mde.FDR < 0.05) & (mde.log2FC > 1); m_down = (mde.FDR < 0.05) & (mde.log2FC < -1)
print('miRNAs tested:', len(mde), '| up:', m_up.sum(), '| down:', m_down.sum())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5.5))
mde['y'] = -np.log10(mde.FDR)
ax.scatter(mde.log2FC, mde.y, s=10, color='lightgrey')

ax.scatter(mde[m_down].log2FC, mde[m_down].y, s=12, color='#2e86c1', label=f'Down ({m_down.sum()})')
mde['name'] = mde.index.str.replace('hsa-', '')
add_labels(ax, mde.loc[mde[m_up].nlargest(8, 'log2FC').index.union(['hsa-mir-21'])], 'log2FC', 'y', 'name', 'right', gap=1.6)
add_labels(ax, mde[m_down].nsmallest(8, 'log2FC'), 'log2FC', 'y', 'name', 'left', gap=1.6)

ax.axvline(1, color='black', ls='--', lw=0.8); ax.axvline(-1, color='black', ls='--', lw=0.8)
ax.axhline(-np.log10(0.05), color='black', ls='--', lw=0.8)

Interpretation

101 pairs, 354 expressed miRNAs, 48 up and 52 down (FDR < 0.05, ≥ 2-fold).

  • Up: miR-21 (log2FC 2.15) – the best-known "oncomiR", raised in almost every solid cancer; the miR-183/96/182 cluster (2.92, 2.71, 2.16); the miR-200 family / miR-141 / miR-429, guardians of the epithelial state (tumours are epithelial cells, normal breast is mostly fat); miR-210 (2.87), switched on by hypoxia – tumours outgrow their blood supply.
  • Down: miR-139, miR-145, miR-204 – reported tumour-suppressor miRNAs; and miR-451a, miR-144, miR-486 (-3.89) – miRNAs made in red blood cells: again a composition effect, normal tissue holds more blood.
  • The same lesson as for genes: some changes are regulation inside cancer cells, others are the changed cell mixture.

Multi-omics integration

Executed notebook CII_03_Multiomics_Integration_INSTRUCTOR.ipynb: code, real output, figures and interpretation.

Multi-omics integration: do the layers tell the same story?

The central dogma: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein, with miRNAs binding mRNAs and reducing their translation or stability. With all three layers measured on the same tumours we can ask:

  1. Does a subtype look the same in mRNA and in protein?
  2. How well does mRNA predict protein, gene by gene?
  3. Do miRNAs and their target genes move in opposite directions?
  4. Does each layer, alone and combined, group tumours by subtype?

Files needed (Colab): from processed/ (made by Notebook 1): mrna_logcpm_tumours.csv.gz, mirna_tumours.csv.gz, protein_tumours.csv.gz, samples_qc.csv.

Step 2 · The two key breast-cancer drivers in two layers

Treatment decisions rest on two proteins: the estrogen receptor (ER, gene ESR1) and HER2 (gene ERBB2). RPPA antibody names are not gene symbols: ER-α protein is called ERALPHA, HER2 is HER2.

    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel(''); ax.set_ylabel('log2 CPM' if 'mRNA' in title else 'RPPA level')
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('03_er_her2_two_layers'); plt.show()

print(pd.DataFrame({t: v.groupby(subtype).median() for t, v in panels}).loc[order].round(2))
Output
               ESR1 mRNA  ER-alpha protein  ERBB2 mRNA  HER2 protein
pam50_subtype                                                       
LumA                9.22              2.27        8.61          0.09
LumB                9.39              2.48        8.44          0.27
Her2                3.89             -0.74       11.91          2.31
Basal               2.69             -1.30        7.57         -0.23
Interpretation
  • ER axis: LumA and LumB have high ESR1 mRNA and high ER-α protein; Basal-like tumours have almost none (median ESR1 9.22 vs 2.69 log2 CPM). This is why Basal-like ≈ "triple-negative" and why hormone therapy works for luminal but not basal tumours.
  • HER2 axis: the HER2-enriched group stands far above the rest in both ERBB2 mRNA and HER2 protein. In these tumours the ERBB2 gene is amplified (many DNA copies) → more mRNA → more protein: one event visible in every layer, and the target of trastuzumab.
  • The two layers agree in pattern, but the protein boxes overlap more – protein measurement is noisier and adds regulation of its own.

Step 3 · How well does mRNA predict protein?

First the two famous genes, then every gene–protein pair we can match. We skip phospho-proteins (names with _p) because phosphorylation is a modification, not an amount of protein.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2))
for ax, (g, p) in zip(axes, [('ESR1', 'ERALPHA'), ('ERBB2', 'HER2')]):

        idx = subtype.index[subtype == s]
        ax.scatter(mrna.loc[g, idx], protein.loc[p, idx], s=8, alpha=0.6, color=COLORS[s], label=s)

    ax.set_xlabel(f'{g} mRNA (log2 CPM)'); ax.set_ylabel(f'{p} protein (RPPA)'); ax.set_title(f'r = {r:.2f}')
axes[0].legend(markerscale=2, fontsize=8)

    HER2 ERBB2  0.80
CYCLINE1 CCNE1  0.79

Interpretation
  • ER: r = 0.89 and HER2: r = 0.8 – for these driver genes, mRNA tells you the protein level very well. The HER2 plot shows two clouds: amplified tumours (top right) and the rest.
  • Across all 204 matched pairs, however, the median correlation is only 0.34; 44 % of pairs have r < 0.3, and a few are even negative. This is a classic multi-omics finding: mRNA is an imperfect proxy for protein. Reasons: translation rate, protein degradation, post-translational modification, and antibody quality.
  • The best-agreeing pairs (ERALPHA 0.89, GATA3 0.82, BCL2 0.82, AR 0.82, HER2 0.80) are proteins whose amount is set mainly by how much the gene is transcribed, measured with very good antibodies. Signalling proteins controlled after translation agree poorly.
  • Practical message: if a decision depends on a protein (ER, HER2), measure the protein – as pathologists do with IHC.

Step 4 · miRNAs and their target genes

A miRNA that represses a gene should show a negative correlation with it across tumours. Two well-studied pairs:

  • miR-200c / miR-141 → ZEB1: the miR-200 family keeps cells epithelial by silencing ZEB1, a driver of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), the step towards invasion.
  • miR-18a → ESR1: miR-18a binds the ESR1 mRNA.

And one warning example: miR-155 vs SOCS1 (a reported target).

pairs = [('hsa-mir-200c', 'ZEB1'), ('hsa-mir-141', 'ZEB1'), ('hsa-mir-18a', 'ESR1'), ('hsa-mir-155', 'SOCS1')]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(17, 3.9))
mirna_r = {}
for ax, (mi, g) in zip(axes, pairs):
    for s in order:
        idx = subtype.index[subtype == s]
        ax.scatter(mirna.loc[mi, idx], mrna.loc[g, idx], s=6, alpha=0.5, color=COLORS[s], label=s)
    r = np.corrcoef(mirna.loc[mi], mrna.loc[g])[0, 1]
    mirna_r[(mi, g)] = r
    ax.set_xlabel(mi.replace('hsa-', '') + ' (log2 RPM)'); ax.set_ylabel(g + ' mRNA (log2 CPM)'); ax.set_title(f'r = {r:.2f}')
axes[0].legend(markerscale=2, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('03_mirna_vs_targets'); plt.show()

immune = ['PTPRC', 'CD3E', 'CD8A', 'MS4A1']
print('miR-155 vs immune-cell genes:', {g: round(np.corrcoef(mirna.loc['hsa-mir-155'], mrna.loc[g])[0, 1], 2) for g in immune})
print('SOCS1  vs immune-cell genes:', {g: round(np.corrcoef(mrna.loc['SOCS1'], mrna.loc[g])[0, 1], 2) for g in immune})
Output
miR-155 vs immune-cell genes: {'PTPRC': np.float64(0.61), 'CD3E': np.float64(0.7), 'CD8A': np.float64(0.65), 'MS4A1': np.float64(0.59)}
SOCS1  vs immune-cell genes: {'PTPRC': np.float64(0.49), 'CD3E': np.float64(0.69), 'CD8A': np.float64(0.63), 'MS4A1': np.float64(0.55)}
Interpretation
  • miR-200c ↔ ZEB1: r = -0.37; miR-141 ↔ ZEB1: r = -0.39 – negative, as expected for a miRNA that represses its target. Tumours with little miR-200 express more ZEB1 (a more mesenchymal, invasive programme).
  • miR-18a ↔ ESR1: r = -0.62 – the strongest of all. Basal-like tumours (green) have high miR-18a and very low ESR1. But ESR1 is also low in basal tumours for other reasons, so the correlation is partly the subtype difference itself.
  • miR-155 ↔ SOCS1: r = +0.57 – positive, although SOCS1 is a reported miR-155 target. Both are made by immune cells: miR-155 correlates with the immune-cell genes PTPRC, CD3E, CD8A and MS4A1 (r ≈ 0.64), and so does SOCS1. More lymphocytes in a tumour → more of both. Correlation in bulk tissue ≠ targeting: it can come from a shared cell type. Proving a target needs experiments (reporter assays, knock-downs).

Step 5 · Each layer alone, and all layers together (PCA)

To integrate we must put the layers on a common footing:

  1. Standardise every feature (mean 0, SD 1), so no layer wins just because of its units.
  2. Weight each block by 1/√(number of features), so mRNA (2,000 features) does not drown the 341 miRNAs and 463 proteins.
  3. Put the blocks side by side (concatenate) and run one PCA. This is early integration; methods such as MOFA or DIABLO (mixOmics) are more advanced versions of the same idea.

We use the 2,000 most variable genes, all miRNAs and all proteins.

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

top_genes = mrna.var(axis=1).nlargest(2000).index
blocks = {'mRNA': mrna.loc[top_genes].T, 'miRNA': mirna.T, 'Protein': protein.T}    # samples as rows

scaled = {}
for name, X in blocks.items():
    scaled[name] = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) / np.sqrt(X.shape[1])
scaled['Integrated'] = np.hstack([scaled['mRNA'], scaled['miRNA'], scaled['Protein']])
for name, Z in scaled.items():
    print(f'{name:10s} {Z.shape[1]:5d} features')
Output
mRNA        2000 features
miRNA        341 features
Protein      463 features
Integrated  2804 features
labelled = subtype.isin(order).values
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 4.4))
pca_res, knn_agree = {}, {}
for ax, (name, Z) in zip(axes, scaled.items()):
    pca = PCA(n_components=10).fit(Z)
    pcs = pca.transform(Z)
    pca_res[name] = pca.explained_variance_ratio_
    ax.scatter(pcs[~labelled, 0], pcs[~labelled, 1], s=5, color='lightgrey', label='no label')
    for s in order:
        m = (subtype == s).values
        ax.scatter(pcs[m, 0], pcs[m, 1], s=7, alpha=0.7, color=COLORS[s], label=s)
    ax.set_title(name); ax.set_xlabel(f'PC1 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]*100:.0f} %)')
    ax.set_ylabel(f'PC2 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]*100:.0f} %)')
    # how often are a tumour's 10 nearest neighbours (in 10-PC space) of the same subtype?
    P = pcs[labelled]; y = subtype[labelled].values
    nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=11).fit(P).kneighbors(P, return_distance=False)[:, 1:]
    knn_agree[name] = (y[nn] == y[:, None]).mean()
axes[0].legend(markerscale=2.5, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('03_pca_layers_integrated'); plt.show()

chance = (subtype[labelled].value_counts(normalize=True) ** 2).sum()
print('Neighbour agreement (same subtype among 10 nearest tumours):')
print({k: round(v, 2) for k, v in knn_agree.items()}, '| expected by chance:', round(chance, 2))
Output
Neighbour agreement (same subtype among 10 nearest tumours):
{'mRNA': np.float64(0.77), 'miRNA': np.float64(0.65), 'Protein': np.float64(0.62), 'Integrated': np.float64(0.74)} | expected by chance: 0.34
Interpretation
  • In the mRNA and the integrated view, Basal-like tumours (green) form a clearly separate group. In the miRNA and protein views the first two PCs mix the subtypes more: the biggest sources of variation there are other things (e.g. immune and stromal content, technical batch), and the subtype signal lies in later components.
  • Luminal A and B overlap: they are two ends of a continuum (mainly how fast the cells divide), not two clean islands.
  • Neighbour agreement (how often a tumour's 10 nearest neighbours share its subtype): mRNA 0.77, miRNA 0.65, protein 0.62, integrated 0.74; chance would be 0.34. All layers carry subtype information. mRNA carries the most – unsurprising, because PAM50 subtypes were defined from mRNA. The integrated view sits between the layers: combining helps most when layers carry different information about the question, and here mRNA already holds most of it.

Step 6 · A multi-omics heatmap of subtype markers

For each layer we pick the 12 features that differ most between subtypes (ANOVA F-test) and show them together, tumours ordered by subtype.

from sklearn.feature_selection import f_classif

lab_idx = subtype.index[subtype.isin(order)]
y = subtype[lab_idx]
picked = []
for name, X in [('mRNA', mrna.loc[top_genes]), ('miRNA', mirna), ('Protein', protein)]:
    F, _ = f_classif(X[lab_idx].T, y)
    best = pd.Series(F, index=X.index).nlargest(12).index
    z = X.loc[best, lab_idx]
    z = z.sub(z.mean(axis=1), axis=0).div(z.std(axis=1), axis=0)
    z.index = [f'{name}: {i.replace("hsa-", "")}' for i in best]
    picked.append(z)
heat = pd.concat(picked)
col_order = pd.concat([y[y == s] for s in order]).index
heat = heat[col_order]

col_colors = pd.Series([COLORS[s] for s in y[col_order]], index=col_order, name='subtype')
g = sns.clustermap(heat, row_cluster=False, col_cluster=False, col_colors=col_colors, cmap='RdBu_r',
                   vmin=-2.5, vmax=2.5, xticklabels=False, figsize=(13, 10),
                   cbar_pos=(0.01, 0.80, 0.02, 0.12), dendrogram_ratio=(0.02, 0.04))
for i in [12, 24]:
    g.ax_heatmap.axhline(i, color='black', lw=1.5)
g.ax_heatmap.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=8)
g.ax_heatmap.set_xlabel('Tumours ordered by subtype:  ' + '  |  '.join(order) + '   (colour bar on top)')
g.savefig(f'{ROOT}/results/figures/03_multiomics_heatmap.png', dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight'); plt.show()
print(heat.index.tolist())
Output
['mRNA: FOXA1', 'mRNA: MLPH', 'mRNA: ESR1', 'mRNA: FOXC1', 'mRNA: AGR3', 'mRNA: CA12', 'mRNA: SPDEF', 'mRNA: C5AR2', 'mRNA: TBC1D9', 'mRNA: GATA3', 'mRNA: XBP1', 'mRNA: CCDC170', 'miRNA: mir-18a', 'miRNA: mir-135b', 'miRNA: mir-190b', 'miRNA: mir-17', 'miRNA: mir-505', 'miRNA: mir-106b', 'miRNA: mir-130b', 'miRNA: mir-20a', 'miRNA: mir-590', 'miRNA: mir-197', 'miRNA: mir-942', 'miRNA: mir-19a', 'Protein: ERALPHA', 'Protein: GATA3', 'Protein: AR', 'Protein: ASNS', 'Protein: FOXM1', 'Protein: INPP4B', 'Protein: CYCLINE1', 'Protein: CYCLINB1', 'Protein: PLK1', 'Protein: CDK1_pT14', 'Protein: BCL2', 'Protein: PHGDH']
Interpretation

Reading the three blocks together tells one coherent story per subtype:

  • Luminal A / B (left): the estrogen-receptor programme is on in mRNA (FOXA1, ESR1, GATA3, XBP1, AGR3, SPDEF) and in protein (ER-α, GATA3, AR, INPP4B, BCL2); miR-190b (a miRNA known to be high in ER-positive tumours) is high.
  • Basal-like (right): that whole luminal block is blue (off). FOXC1 – a known basal-like transcription factor – is on; the miR-17~92 family (miR-17, -18a, -19a, -20a, -106b) is high; and the proliferation proteins FOXM1, Cyclin E1, Cyclin B1 and PLK1 are high: fast-dividing tumours.
  • Luminal B and HER2-enriched sit in between: luminal markers partly on, proliferation proteins partly up.

Three independent technologies (sequencing of mRNA, sequencing of miRNA, antibodies for protein) agree on the same structure – strong evidence that the subtypes are real biology, not an artefact of one assay. Top features by ANOVA: mRNA – FOXA1, MLPH, ESR1; miRNA – mir-18a, mir-135b, mir-190b; protein – ERALPHA, GATA3, AR.

NOTEBOOK 4 OF 4

Machine learning: predicting the subtype

Executed notebook CII_04_Machine_Learning_INSTRUCTOR.ipynb: code, real output, figures and interpretation.

Machine learning: predicting the breast-cancer subtype from omics data

Task 1 (main): predict the PAM50 subtype (LumA, LumB, HER2-enriched, Basal-like) of a tumour from (a) mRNA, (b) miRNA, (c) protein, (d) all three layers together. Which layer predicts best? Does combining help?

Task 2: predict ER status as judged by a pathologist (IHC) – a label measured by a completely different method.

Pitfall demo: how "data leakage" produces impressive but fake accuracy.

The machine-learning workflow

  1. Features X (samples × features) and labels y
  2. Split once into training (75 %) and test (25 %) sets – the test set is locked away until the very end
  3. On the training set: cross-validation (5 folds) to estimate performance and compare models
  4. Fit the chosen model on the whole training set, then evaluate once on the test set
  5. Interpret: which features drive the predictions? Do they make biological sense?

Files needed (Colab): from processed/: mrna_logcpm_tumours.csv.gz, mirna_tumours.csv.gz, protein_tumours.csv.gz, samples_qc.csv.

Step 1 · Features (X) and labels (y)

Machine learning wants samples as rows, so we transpose each layer. We prefix every feature with its layer (mRNA:ESR1, miRNA:mir-18a, Protein:ERALPHA) so we always know where it came from.

mrna    = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/processed/mrna_logcpm_tumours.csv.gz', index_col=0)
mirna   = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/processed/mirna_tumours.csv.gz', index_col=0)
protein = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/processed/protein_tumours.csv.gz', index_col=0)
samples = pd.read_csv(f'{ROOT}/processed/samples_qc.csv', index_col=0)

layers = {'mRNA':    mrna.T.add_prefix('mRNA:'),
          'miRNA':   mirna.T.rename(columns=lambda c: 'miRNA:' + c.replace('hsa-', '')),
          'Protein': protein.T.add_prefix('Protein:')}
subtype = samples.loc[mrna.columns, 'pam50_subtype']

classes = ['LumA', 'LumB', 'Her2', 'Basal']
y = subtype[subtype.isin(classes)]                     # labelled tumours (Normal-like and missing left out)
unlabelled = subtype.index[subtype.isna()]
print('Labelled tumours:', len(y), '| without label:', len(unlabelled))
print(y.value_counts())

Step 2 · Split once: training set and a locked test set

stratify=y keeps the subtype proportions the same in both sets. random_state makes the split reproducible.

train_ids, test_ids = train_test_split(y.index, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=SEED)
print('Training:', len(train_ids), '| Test:', len(test_ids))
pd.DataFrame({'train': y[train_ids].value_counts(normalize=True).round(2),
              'test':  y[test_ids].value_counts(normalize=True).round(2)})

# Build the four feature tables. For mRNA we keep the 2,000 most variable genes,
# choosing them on the TRAINING samples only (the test set must not influence any choice).
top_genes = layers['mRNA'].loc[train_ids].var().nlargest(2000).index
X_sets = {'mRNA': layers['mRNA'][top_genes], 'miRNA': layers['miRNA'], 'Protein': layers['Protein']}
X_sets['All three'] = pd.concat([X_sets['mRNA'], X_sets['miRNA'], X_sets['Protein']], axis=1)
for name, X in X_sets.items():
    print(f'{name:10s} {X.shape[1]:5d} features')

Step 3 · Two models, four feature sets

  • Logistic regression inside a pipeline: StandardScaler (mean 0, SD 1) → SelectKBest (keep the 200 features that best separate the classes, ANOVA F-test) → LogisticRegression (a linear model; C=0.05 = strong regularisation, which shrinks unhelpful weights – important when features ≫ samples). Because selection happens inside the pipeline, it is redone inside every cross-validation fold → no leakage.
  • Random forest: 500 decision trees, each on a random subset of samples and features; the forest votes.

Balanced accuracy = average of the per-class accuracies (fair with unbalanced classes; chance = 0.25 for 4 classes).

def make_models():
    return {
        'Logistic regression': make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(f_classif, k=200),
                                             LogisticRegression(C=0.05, max_iter=5000)),
        'Random forest': RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, class_weight='balanced',
                                                random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1),
    }

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
rows, fitted = [], {}
for set_name, X in X_sets.items():
    for model_name, model in make_models().items():
        cv_scores = cross_val_score(model, X.loc[train_ids], y[train_ids], cv=cv, scoring='balanced_accuracy')
        model.fit(X.loc[train_ids], y[train_ids])                 # final fit on all training data
        pred = model.predict(X.loc[test_ids])                     # first and only look at the test set
        fitted[(set_name, model_name)] = model
        rows.append([set_name, model_name, cv_scores.mean(), cv_scores.std(),
                     balanced_accuracy_score(y[test_ids], pred), accuracy_score(y[test_ids], pred),
                     f1_score(y[test_ids], pred, average='macro')])
results = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['features', 'model', 'CV balanced acc', 'CV SD',
                                      'Test balanced acc', 'Test accuracy', 'Test macro-F1'])
results.to_csv(f'{ROOT}/results/tables/ml_subtype_results.csv', index=False)
results.round(3)
Output

plot.plot(kind='bar', ax=ax, color=['#34495e', '#95a5a6'], rot=0, width=0.7)
ax.axhline(0.25, color='black', ls=':', lw=1); ax.text(3.45, 0.27, 'chance', ha='right', fontsize=8)

Interpretation

All models are far above chance (0.25). Test balanced accuracy, logistic regression: mRNA 0.86, miRNA 0.70, protein 0.75, all three 0.85 (random forest: 0.86 / 0.61 / 0.72 / 0.87).

  • mRNA predicts best – but read this carefully. PAM50 subtypes were defined from the mRNA of 50 genes. Predicting them from mRNA is partly circular: the model largely re-discovers the definition. It proves the pipeline works, not that mRNA is "the best biomarker".
  • Protein and miRNA – measured by different technologies – still recover the subtype well. That is the more interesting result: the subtypes are real at several molecular levels.
  • Combining all three gave about the same as mRNA alone (logistic regression 0.85 vs 0.86; random forest 0.87 vs 0.86). Integration helps when layers carry complementary information about the target; here mRNA already contains most of it. An honest "no gain" is still a result.
  • For mRNA and all-three, cross-validation (training set) and test scores agree within a few points. For miRNA and protein the test score is 5–10 points lower than CV: with only 160 test tumours (15 of them HER2-enriched) a few errors move balanced accuracy a lot – single test-set estimates are noisy, which is why we also report CV ± SD.
  • The simple linear model is as good as the forest overall and better for miRNA and protein: with few samples and many features, simple regularised models often win.

Interpretation
  • Basal-like is almost never confused with anything (recall 0.93 with all three layers): it is biologically the most distinct subtype, as the PCA showed.
  • Most errors are LumA ↔ LumB (11 of 17 errors in the all-layers model). This is not a failure of the model: Luminal A and B lie on a continuum of proliferation (cell-division rate), and the cut-off between them is somewhat arbitrary. Pathologists face the same grey zone with Ki-67 staining.
  • HER2-enriched has the lowest recall (0.73): it is the smallest class (15 test tumours), and some HER2-amplified tumours look luminal in their other genes.

Step 5 · Opening the black box: which features drive the predictions?

For logistic regression every class has one weight (coefficient) per selected feature. A raw weight can mislead, because correlated features share and even swap weight. A fairer measure of what the model uses for a class:

contribution = weight × the average (standardised) value of that feature in the class's own tumours.

A large positive contribution means "this feature pushes the class's own tumours towards the right answer". The arrow shows whether the feature is high (↑) or low (↓) in that class – a class can be recognised by what is switched off as much as by what is switched on.

scaler   = best.named_steps['standardscaler']
selector = best.named_steps['selectkbest']
logreg   = best.named_steps['logisticregression']
selected = X_sets['All three'].columns[selector.get_support()]

Z = pd.DataFrame(selector.transform(scaler.transform(X_sets['All three'].loc[train_ids])),
                 index=train_ids, columns=selected)                     # standardised training data
class_mean = Z.groupby(y[train_ids]).mean()                             # average z-value per class
weights = pd.DataFrame(logreg.coef_, index=logreg.classes_, columns=selected)
contribution = weights * class_mean.loc[weights.index]

top_features = {}
for c in classes:
    best6 = contribution.loc[c].nlargest(6).index
    top_features[c] = [f"{f} {'↑' if class_mean.at[c, f] > 0 else '↓'}" for f in best6]
pd.DataFrame(top_features)

Selected features by layer (of 200): {'mRNA': 188, 'miRNA': 6, 'Protein': 6}
Random forest importance share by layer: {'Protein': 0.08, 'mRNA': 0.87, 'miRNA': 0.06}
Share of features by layer:             {'mRNA': 0.71, 'Protein': 0.17, 'miRNA': 0.12}

Random forest top 12: ['mRNA:ESR1', 'mRNA:FOXC1', 'Protein:ERALPHA', 'mRNA:TTC6', 'mRNA:C5AR2', 'mRNA:CCDC170', 'mRNA:TFF3', 'mRNA:XBP1', 'mRNA:AGR2', 'mRNA:SPDEF', 'mRNA:RGMA', 'mRNA:GREB1']
Interpretation

The model's main "reasons" per class (↑ high / ↓ low in that class):

  • LumA: EXO1 ↓, NDC80 ↓, BIRC5 ↓, CDC45 ↓, BCAM ↑, MAPT ↑
  • LumB: SFRP1 ↓, FOXC1 ↓, TRIM29 ↓, CRYAB ↓, KRT6B ↓, PPP1R14C ↓
  • Her2: PADI2 ↑, protein ERALPHA ↓, C5AR2 ↓, RERG ↓, ESR1 ↓, CCDC170 ↓
  • Basal: FOXC1 ↑, PPP1R14C ↑, GPR160 ↓, BCAS1 ↓, AR ↓, CAPN13 ↓

Read as biology:

  • Luminal A is recognised mostly by low proliferation genes (EXO1, NDC80, BIRC5, CDC45 – cell-division genes) together with luminal-type genes such as MAPT and BCAM being high: a slowly dividing, hormone-driven tumour.
  • Luminal B is recognised by the basal markers being off (SFRP1, FOXC1, TRIM29, CRYAB, KRT6B low). What separates it from LumA (faster division) is subtler – which is exactly where the confusion matrix showed most errors.
  • HER2-enriched is separated from the luminal tumours by the estrogen-receptor programme being off (ESR1 ↓, ER-α protein ↓, and the estrogen-driven genes RERG and CCDC170 ↓).
  • Basal-like is recognised by the basal transcription factor FOXC1 and PPP1R14C being on, and the androgen receptor AR and luminal genes (BCAS1, CAPN13) being off.

When a model's reasons match known biology we can trust it more; if it relied on, say, a batch-specific gene, we should worry. Note that one protein (ER-α) appears among the top reasons, but mRNA dominates.

Of the 200 features selected, 188 are mRNA, 6 miRNA and 6 protein. In the random forest the mRNA block carries 87 % of the total importance (while making up 71 % of the features): the model leans on mRNA, consistent with the circularity noted above.

Step 6 · An independent label: ER status judged by a pathologist (IHC)

PAM50 comes from mRNA, so Task 1 is partly circular. ER status by immunohistochemistry is decided by a pathologist looking at a stained slide – a different measurement altogether. Can each omics layer reproduce the pathologist's call? We use the ROC curve and AUC (1 = perfect, 0.5 = coin toss).

er = samples.loc[mrna.columns, 'ER_status_IHC']
er = er[er.isin(['Positive', 'Negative'])]
y_er = (er == 'Positive').astype(int)
tr, te = train_test_split(y_er.index, test_size=0.25, stratify=y_er, random_state=SEED)
print('Tumours with IHC ER status:', len(y_er), '| ER-positive:', y_er.sum(), '| ER-negative:', (y_er == 0).sum())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5))
auc, probs = {}, {}
for set_name in ['mRNA', 'miRNA', 'Protein', 'All three']:
    X = X_sets[set_name]
    model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(f_classif, k=min(200, X.shape[1])),
                          LogisticRegression(C=0.05, max_iter=5000))
    model.fit(X.loc[tr], y_er[tr])
    probs[set_name] = pd.Series(model.predict_proba(X.loc[te])[:, 1], index=te)
    auc[set_name] = roc_auc_score(y_er[te], probs[set_name])
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_er[te], probs[set_name])
    ax.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f'{set_name}  AUC = {auc[set_name]:.3f}')
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k:', lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel('False positive rate (ER-neg called positive)'); ax.set_ylabel('True positive rate (ER-pos found)')
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='lower right'); plt.tight_layout(); save_fig('04_er_roc'); plt.show()

print('Test tumours:', len(te), '| confident disagreements:', len(confident_disagree))

IHC model P(ER+) ESR1 mRNA ER-alpha protein PAM50

TCGA-A2-A1G6-01A Negative 0.962 8.4 -0.27 Normal
